justification: None of the provided articles examine bipolar disorder at all; there are no genetic association studies, case reports, or family studies linking CUL4A variants to bipolar disorder or any affective phenotype. The corpus is dominated by CRL4/CUL4A ubiquitin ligase biochemistry, cancer prognosis, inflammation, DNA repair, and related non-psychiatric topics (PMIDs 17079684, 16951172, 22649780, 31535245). The only tangential neuro-relevant items are CUL4B mutations causing X-linked intellectual disability (PMID 20064923) — a different gene — and an epigenome-wide methylation study of cognitive function in twins that lists CUL4A among thousands of CpG-annotated genes (PMID 33131831), which is incidental and not bipolar-specific. This gives at most a very weak biological rationale (CRL4 function in neurodevelopment), justifying a modest Hypothesized weight, with most probability on Novel and essentially none on Established.

No articles were provided linking ZNF765 to type 2 diabetes, so there is no literature evidence of variants, expression data, or functional/pathway relevance. ZNF765 is a poorly characterized KRAB zinc-finger gene with no documented role in glucose metabolism or beta-cell biology in the supplied material. With zero supporting citations, the relationship is best described as Novel, with small residual probability that unretrieved GWAS or expression evidence exists.

None of the provided articles mention asthma, airway inflammation, or any respiratory phenotype in connection with SRGAP2. The literature focuses almost exclusively on SRGAP2's role in neuronal migration, synaptic development, and human-specific gene duplication (PMIDs 39352808, 31822692, 39406239, 23782070, 22106086), plus scattered reports on osteoclastogenesis, breast cancer, male fertility, lipid variability, and islet gene networks. The only tangential immune/inflammatory links are Rac1-mediated inflammatory osteoclastogenesis in mice (PMID 31880824) and a general review noting srGAP roles in inflammation (PMID 29097383), which provide no mechanistic bridge to asthma. There is no human genetic variant evidence connecting SRGAP2 to asthma or any recognized asthma precursor, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded; a small weight is retained for Hypothesized because of generic inflammatory-pathway biology.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant in CREB5 associated with atrial fibrillation in humans; the human genetic studies involving CREB5 concern Alzheimer's disease, achalasia, restless legs syndrome, ovarian and breast cancer, and myasthenia gravis (PMIDs 32755048, 34197731, 31788832, 26424751, 28096648, 37254650). The "AF" appearing in the annulus fibrosus single-cell papers (PMIDs 36568849, 42790727) is a homonym acronym for annulus fibrosus, not atrial fibrillation, and must be dismissed. The only cardiac-relevant item is a murine/nanoparticle study implicating a KLF2/CREB5/HIF-1α/PFKFB3 axis in cardiac fibroblast metabolic reprogramming and post-infarction myocardial fibrosis (PMID 42293728); atrial fibrosis is a recognized substrate for atrial fibrillation, which gives a weak, indirect biological rationale but is non-human and not about arrhythmia. Therefore the relationship is best judged Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized based on that indirect cardiac fibrosis biology.

None of the provided articles report any association or functional link between LMTK2 and type 2 diabetes; the literature focuses on neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's, axonal transport, tau), CFTR/chloride transport in cystic fibrosis, prostate cancer susceptibility, deafness/limb malformation, and general kinase biology. The only metabolically relevant human genetic study is the multi-population gene–educational attainment lipid GWAS (PMID 38028628), which implicates an LMTK2 locus in HDL/LDL/TG levels — dyslipidemia is a correlated cardiometabolic trait but not a definitive precursor or established mechanism of type 2 diabetes, so it provides only weak partial support for "Existing." No study demonstrates variants in LMTK2 in diabetic probands or families, so "Established" is excluded. Mechanistic work (trafficking, kinesin-1/Smad2/TGF-β signalling, CFTR endocytosis) is not directly tied to insulin secretion or glucose homeostasis, giving only marginal grounds for "Hypothesized." The bulk of the probability therefore falls on "Novel."

None of the provided articles mention schizophrenia at all, and no study reports MYO18A variants in schizophrenia probands or families. The disease associations described involve Ménière's disease, Alzheimer's disease marker/pathway analyses, West syndrome candidate genes, myeloproliferative syndrome fusion (MYO18A-FGFR1), Hirschsprung's disease, and cardiomyopathy, none of which are recognized precursors or subtypes of schizophrenia. Some indirect biological plausibility exists because MYO18A appears among neurodevelopmental/epileptic encephalopathy candidate genes alongside CYFIP1/CYFIP2 and is expressed in brain tissue, which provides at most a weak hypothetical basis. Overall the evidence base supports a Novel classification, with a modest allowance for Hypothesized given cytoskeletal/neuronal biology.

None of the supplied articles examines bipolar disorder or any psychiatric phenotype in relation to SSBP2; the literature is dominated by cancer biology (hepatocellular carcinoma, glioblastoma survival, skin cancer, head and neck cancer), DNA-binding/telomere biology, Wnt enhanceosome structure, protein C levels, and kidney malformations. The only neurologically relevant items are a mouse BXD study identifying Ssbp2 as a cis-regulated candidate for adult hippocampal neurogenesis (PMID 16407118) and a Mendelian randomization study where an educational-attainment locus containing SSBP2 (among LRRC2 and NEGR1) related to Alzheimer risk (PMID 30863791) — these give a weak, indirect biological rationale for a brain role but do not implicate bipolar disorder. No human genetic association with bipolar disorder, in any proband or family, is reported, so Established is untenable and Existing is nearly unsupported. Some probability is retained for Hypothesized because neurogenesis/neurodevelopmental relevance and a brain-expressed transcriptional cofactor role could be argued as a plausible mechanism. The dominant answer is Novel, since co-mentions are incidental.

None of the provided articles study asthma or any asthma-related respiratory phenotype. UBAC2 variants are reported in Behçet's disease (PMIDs 21918955, 22455605, 28389674), basal/squamous cell carcinoma (21700618), multiple sclerosis (42194988) and tinnitus (39543288), none of which are precursors, subtypes, or recognized risk factors for asthma. The only conceivable link is generic immunological/inflammatory biology: UBAC2 acts as an ER-phagy receptor restraining inflammatory responses (39284914) and regulates lymphopoiesis via Wnt/β-catenin (31073040), which could loosely support a hypothesized role in allergic inflammation, but these are mouse/in vitro mechanistic studies without any asthma readout. Therefore Established and Existing are essentially unsupported, with most weight on Novel and a modest allowance for Hypothesized based on immune-regulatory biology.

None of the provided articles report an association between RAB5B variants and adult height; the corpus is dominated by PCOS genetics at the 12q13.2 locus (RPS26/RAB5B/SUOX), vesicular trafficking biology, surfactant protein maturation, and neurodegeneration. The only anthropometric-adjacent human evidence is the proteome-wide/SMR analysis linking RAB5B protein to birth weight and cortical structure (PMID 40044659), which is a growth-related trait but not adult height itself, and it is a single unreplicated report. The PCOS association studies (PMIDs 27217259, 24106282, 25904635, 36423778) identify variants in a multi-gene region that cannot single out RAB5B and concern a reproductive/metabolic phenotype, not stature. Remaining papers describe RAB5B endosomal function in cells and mouse models, which could at most support a hypothesized role via growth-factor receptor trafficking (e.g., ERBB3/MET signaling), not a height-specific link. Therefore Novel is most likely, with some weight to Existing because of the birth-weight PWAS finding.

None of the provided articles mention schizophrenia at all. CYP7B1 evidence in these papers concerns hereditary spastic paraplegia type 5 (SPG5), congenital bile acid synthesis disorder type 3, osteoarthritis via the CH25H-CYP7B1-RORα axis, and oxysterol-mediated inflammation in viral infection. The only tangential neuropsychiatric relevance is CYP7B1's role in brain oxysterol/cholesterol metabolism and neurodegeneration biomarkers (PMID 21515244), which could support a weak biological hypothesis but is not directed at schizophrenia. There are no human genetic association or causal studies linking CYP7B1 variants to schizophrenia, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded, and the co-mentions are incidental, favoring Novel.

None of the supplied articles examines adult height or any growth/stature phenotype. The structural and biochemical papers (PMIDs 41959150, 33084328) characterize ATAD2B as a bromodomain-containing AAA+ ATPase involved in chromatin recognition, providing no link to skeletal growth. The toxicogenomics study (PMID 22208759) lists ATAD2B among 12 differentially expressed genes in POP-exposed girls, with pathway software vaguely implicating connective tissue/skeletal muscular disorders—this is an incidental co-mention, not evidence of variant-based association with adult height. No human genetic variant studies, families, probands, or cohorts connecting ATAD2B to height are present, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported; only a very weak, speculative biological rationale exists for Hypothesized.

No article reports MICU2 variants in human probands or families with atrial fibrillation; the only human MICU2 loss-of-function report (PMID 29053821) describes a neurodevelopmental disorder, not arrhythmia. The strongest link is the Micu2-/- mouse (PMID 29073106), which shows left atrial enlargement, impaired cardiomyocyte relaxation and diastolic dysfunction—well-recognized substrates for atrial fibrillation—plus elevated MICU2 expression in human and murine cardiovascular pathology transcriptomes (expression correlation, not genetic variation). Additional papers establish MICU2's role as a gatekeeper of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter and its relevance to cardiac calcium handling, energetics and ischemia/reperfusion (PMIDs 39185387, 31533452, 28273446, 24503055), providing a plausible mechanistic basis for atrial remodeling. This constitutes biological/animal-model plausibility rather than human genetic association, so "Hypothesized" is by far the most appropriate category, with a small allowance for "Existing" given the human expression data in cardiovascular disease.

No human study in this set reports variants in CLVS1 associated with BMI, obesity, or adiposity. The human genetic reports concern steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (PMID 34874915) and suicidal ideation in schizophrenia (PMID 30149091), neither of which is a recognized precursor or mechanism for BMI. The only body-size-related finding is a sheep genome-wide association with meat production/ultrasonic carcass traits (PMID 37372468), which is non-human and therefore at best supports a hypothesized, indirect link to body composition. The ccRCC autophagy prognostic signature (PMID 35237298) is an incidental co-mention with no relevance to BMI. Accordingly, weight is split between Novel and Hypothesized, with minimal probability for Existing/Established.

No articles were provided linking KRTAP5-4 to type 2 diabetes. KRTAP5-4 encodes a keratin-associated protein involved in hair follicle keratin cross-linking, with no known biological role in glucose homeostasis, insulin secretion, or insulin sensitivity. Without any supporting literature—genetic, expression, functional, or animal—there is no basis for an established, existing, or even hypothesized relationship. The evidence therefore supports the Novel category.

None of the provided articles mention asthma or any asthma-related phenotype, airway biology, or allergic/immune mechanism. The MBD3L2 literature here concerns neuroendocrine tumor development (PMID 41175375), FSHD muscular dystrophy biomarkers (PMID 23966205), coiled-coil biophysics with p66α/NuRD (PMID 23239876), and Tet2-mediated 5mC oxidation (PMID 26769901). There are no human genetic association studies, variants in probands or families, or even a plausible mechanistic pathway linking MBD3L2 to asthma in this set. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a minimal allowance for a speculative epigenetic-regulation link.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in NMT1 associated with blood pressure, hypertension, or any recognized precursor trait, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only vascular-relevant work is a rat single-cell RNA-seq study of carotid artery injury, where NMT1 was validated as a marker of the synthetic vascular smooth muscle cell phenotype (PMID 34957241) — this is animal/in vitro biology touching on vascular remodeling, which gives some, but indirect, mechanistic plausibility rather than a blood-pressure link. Other papers concern enzymology of N-myristoyltransferase in fungi, plants, bovine tissue, viral infection, cancer, and neurodegeneration, and are incidental co-mentions. A UK Biobank eQTL-imaging study includes NMT1 but relates to white matter microstructure, not blood pressure (PMID 32066731). Overall the evidence is largely absent, favoring Novel with a substantial share to Hypothesized due to the VSMC phenotype-switching finding.

None of the provided articles mention atrial fibrillation or any cardiac/arrhythmia phenotype. The FBXL14 literature here concerns E3 ubiquitin ligase functions in EMT regulation, vimentin and c-Myc degradation, RNA Pol I turnover, and co-repressor dynamics in cancer and stem cell contexts (PMIDs 33801272, 26506454, 32453420, 36372232, 42367945). The only human genetic report is a multigene 1.5 Mb 12p13.33 terminal deletion associated with autism spectrum disorder (PMID 24613754), which cannot implicate FBXL14 specifically and is unrelated to AF. There is no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking FBXL14 to atrial fibrillation, so the relationship is best described as novel, with only a small residual allowance for indirect developmental/transcriptional biology.

The single available article concerns TCEAL1 loss-of-function and Xq22.2 deletions causing an early-onset neurodevelopmental disease trait (hypotonia, intellectual disability, autistic-like behavior, dysmorphism); TCEAL4 appears only as a neighboring gene within multigene contiguous deletions, which cannot isolate its individual contribution. Bipolar disorder is not mentioned or assessed in any of the reported probands, and no variant-level or association evidence links TCEAL4 to bipolar disorder. At most one could argue weak biological plausibility via broad neurobehavioral/neurodevelopmental involvement of the Xq22.2 locus, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized. There are no human genetic studies of TCEAL4 in bipolar disorder, so Established is excluded and Existing is essentially unsupported.

QTMAN corresponds to the queuosine tRNA mannosyltransferase (GTDC1). The only functional study (PMID 37992713) is biochemical and zebrafish-based: qtman knockout fish show shortened body length, linking the gene to post-embryonic growth and body size, which is biologically suggestive for body composition/BMI but is animal, not human genetic evidence. The Ugandan TB fine-mapping study (PMID 30100616) reports human variants in ZEB2/GTDC1 associated with persistent tuberculin skin test negativity, and only notes an epidemiological (non-genetic) association between PTST- and protection from body-mass wasting; the variants themselves were not tested against BMI, so this does not constitute human genetic evidence for BMI. No study reports QTMAN/GTDC1 variants associated with BMI in humans, so Established is excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best. Hypothesized is most appropriate given the growth/body-size phenotype in the knockout model and translational/proteostasis biology.

None of the provided articles examine blood pressure, hypertension, or related hemodynamic traits in relation to PPP2R5E. The human genetic studies cited associate PPP2R5E variants with cancer risk/survival, chronic lymphocytic leukemia outcome, lung cancer, dengue fever, Kawasaki disease IVIG response, type 2 diabetes islet biology, and neurodevelopmental/myopathy phenotypes (PMIDs 19773383, 24204789, 21659360, 29447178, 38259468, 28473845, 39284558) — none of which are recognized precursors or mechanisms of blood pressure regulation. Only very indirect, tenuous links exist (e.g., dengue shock syndrome and Kawasaki vasculitis involve vascular/hemodynamic changes, and PP2A signaling is broadly relevant to vascular smooth muscle), which provides at most weak hypothetical grounding rather than evidence. Therefore the relationship is best judged as Novel, with a modest allowance for a Hypothesized biological rationale via PP2A phosphatase signaling in vascular/endothelial contexts.

Neither provided article examines adult height. The WES study (PMID 33559384) reports NOP16 loss-of-function burden in human neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, an autoimmune phenotype with no recognized relationship to stature, so it cannot support Established or Existing for height. The yeast study (PMID 24312670) concerns the Nop16 ortholog in 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis; ribosome biogenesis/growth control provides only a very indirect, non-human biological rationale that could weakly justify "Hypothesized," but there is no expression, model-organism growth, or pathway analysis tied to human height. With no human height-associated variants cited in these results, the evidence base here is essentially incidental co-mention, favoring Novel with some residual weight on Hypothesized.

The only direct human genetic evidence in this list is the osteoarthritis–metabolic traits multi-omics study (PMID 41167325), which highlights rs34811474 in ANAPC4 as a shared variant across osteoarthritis–metabolic trait pairs (metabolic traits include adiposity measures), consistent with ANAPC4 being a known adiposity/body-fat locus. The air-pollution CKM–sarcopenia multi-omics study (PMID 41270966) adds supportive human evidence by linking ANAPC4 methylation sites to cardiometabolic disease and reduced muscle mass, i.e., body-composition phenotypes, but these are methylation/eQTL-based rather than BMI-specific variant associations. Other human papers (Parkinson's/olfaction, chronic pain–COVID, cleft lip) implicate ANAPC4 loci in unrelated traits and do not address BMI. The remaining literature is non-human or in vitro (cattle conformation, goose beak length, Arabidopsis, C. elegans, mouse Pqbp1, cancer cell lines), supporting at most a hypothesized/biological link to growth and cell-cycle regulation. Because no two independent human studies here report ANAPC4 variants associated specifically with BMI as their own primary result, "Established" is unlikely and "Existing" is the best fit.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking CALHM4 to schizophrenia. CALHM4 is a calcium homeostasis modulator family member with limited neural characterization compared to CALHM1, and no genetic association or functional studies connecting it to schizophrenia are presented here. Without any supporting publications, the relationship must be considered novel, with small residual probability that unlisted biological or GWAS evidence exists.

None of the provided articles address adult height or any growth/stature phenotype. The apparent "H4C16" matches are homonymous: they refer to histone H4 peptide residue ranges (e.g., H4(16-39), H4 16-23) in lupus autoimmunity studies (PMIDs 8676066, 10430616, 21287397) or in molecular dynamics simulations of histone tail–DNA interactions (PMID 24740714), not to the H4C16 gene. No human genetic variants in H4C16 are reported, and no biological pathway connecting the gene to skeletal growth or height is described. Therefore the evidence base is entirely incidental and supports a "Novel" classification.

None of the provided articles mention type 2 diabetes, glucose metabolism, insulin signaling, or any diabetes-related phenotype. The literature on H3Y2 (histone H3.Y) concerns primate-specific histone variant identification, nucleosome structure, chromatin incorporation, stress/cell-cycle responses, and DUX4 target gene activation in FSHD. There are no human genetic association studies, no probands or families, and no functional or pathway data linking this gene to diabetes. A minimal allowance is retained for the generic notion that stress-responsive chromatin regulation could be tangentially relevant, but this is speculative and not supported by any co-mention here.

Neither article addresses asthma or any respiratory/allergic phenotype. One paper concerns Tceal3 as a developmentally upregulated suppressor of axon regeneration in rodent retinal ganglion cells, and the other describes TCEAL1 loss-of-function (with multigene Xq22.2 deletions including TCEAL3) causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome. There is no genetic, expression, or mechanistic link presented between TCEAL3 and asthma, and the deletion data cannot isolate TCEAL3 even for the neurological trait. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

The only provided article is a Drosophila study of cNT5-II orthologues examining neuropsychiatric-relevant phenotypes (habituation learning, locomotor activity, sleep, synaptic morphology), with no human genetic data and no measurement of body mass index or adiposity-related traits. No human cohort, family, or proband evidence links NT5DC4 variants to BMI. The nucleotidase biology described is not directly tied to energy balance or adiposity, though mild locomotor/sleep changes offer only a very tenuous, indirect mechanistic hint. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports a Novel classification, with a small allowance for Hypothesized.

No articles were provided linking TCEAL2 to asthma, so there is no evidence of genetic variants, expression data, or functional/pathway relevance connecting this transcription elongation factor A-like gene to asthma pathogenesis. Without any supporting literature, neither causal (Established) nor associative (Existing) claims can be substantiated, and no biological rationale (Hypothesized) is documented. The relationship is therefore best described as Novel, with a small residual probability that unlisted GWAS or expression studies exist.

No articles were supplied, so there is no retrievable literature linking WASHC2A (FAM21A, a WASH complex subunit involved in endosomal actin nucleation and retromer-mediated trafficking) to blood pressure. Without any human genetic association studies, family or cohort data, an Established or Existing classification cannot be supported. A minor probability is retained for Hypothesized, since WASH complex-mediated endosomal recycling could plausibly affect receptor trafficking relevant to vascular function, but no such argument is documented here. The absence of any co-mention or mechanistic report makes Novel the most likely correct category.

All retrieved articles concern XAGE1A (XAGE-1b/GAGED2) as a cancer/testis antigen in melanoma, lung adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, prostate cancer, and as a minimal residual disease marker in pediatric AML. None of the studies mention bipolar disorder, psychiatric phenotypes, brain expression, or neuronal pathways, and no genetic variant association with bipolar disorder is reported. The only genetic variation discussed (immunoglobulin GM/KM allotypes) relates to humoral anti-tumor immunity, not mood disorders. There is therefore no biological or genetic basis presented linking XAGE1A to bipolar disorder, making "Novel" the appropriate classification.

No articles were provided, so there is no retrievable evidence linking H4C15 (a replication-dependent histone H4 cluster gene) to adult height. Without any human genetic study, family, or cohort data, the criteria for "Established" or "Existing" cannot be met. A small residual probability is allotted to "Hypothesized" because histone genes have general roles in chromatin regulation and growth-related gene expression, which could in principle be argued as biologically relevant, and to "Existing" in case unlisted GWAS signals near the histone cluster exist. The dominant assessment on this evidence base is "Novel."

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking C18orf63 (an uncharacterized open reading frame) to body mass index. Without any human genetic association studies, functional data, expression findings, or animal models, none of the evidence-based categories can be supported. C18orf63 is a poorly characterized gene with no established role in energy balance or adiposity biology. The absence of any supporting citations strongly favors the Novel category.

None of the provided articles examine atrial fibrillation; all concern myocardial infarction or coronary heart disease. OR13G1 (rs1151640) was reported in a multi-stage gene-centric association study of MI (PMID 16175505) and nominally replicated in a familial hypercholesterolemia cohort (PMID 18599554), but was not validated in an independent MI case-control study (PMID 17967605), and OR13G1 is an olfactory receptor with no described cardiac electrophysiological biology. Coronary disease/MI is only a distal risk factor for AF, so the evidence provides at best indirect support, and no study reports AF phenotypes or probands/families with OR13G1 variants. Therefore Established is untenable, and the weight of evidence favors Novel with some allowance for an indirect "Existing" interpretation via the MI risk-factor link.

None of the provided articles report a genetic association between LRRC8E and schizophrenia. The only human genetic study (PMID 27610895) examines panic disorder, finding only a nominal association of rs3745383 in LRRC8E in an isolated Faroese cohort, with no replication in Danish or German cohorts; panic disorder is not a recognized precursor or subtype of schizophrenia, though the authors speculate about shared susceptibility across mental disorders at 19p13.2. The remaining papers (PMIDs 35777784, 33827893, 27325695) concern VRAC/LRRC8 channel biophysics, renal physiology, and cGAMP/cisplatin transport, with no neuropsychiatric relevance presented. There is therefore no causal human evidence (Established is excluded, as no PMID reports schizophrenia probands with LRRC8E variants), and only a tenuous indirect biological rationale (anion/glutamate-releasing channel expressed in brain) supporting a Hypothesized relationship.

None of the provided articles examine adult height or any anthropometric trait. The papers concern ASFV immune evasion via DCST1-mediated STAT2 degradation (PMID: 36856422), a Parkinson's disease GWAS/machine-learning study highlighting a DCST1 missense variant rs11264300 (PMID: 37842648), and sperm–oocyte fusion biology in C. elegans and human spermatozoa (PMIDs: 37453426, 40711049). The human genetic evidence present (Parkinson's disease) is for an unrelated phenotype and is not a recognized precursor or mechanism for adult height, so it cannot support Existing or Established. The biological roles described (fertilization, ubiquitin ligase activity in interferon signaling) provide no plausible pathway to skeletal growth, leaving only incidental co-mention. Therefore the evidence base here is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for height-associated loci reported elsewhere but not documented in these articles.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking BICRAL (GLTSCR1L, a GBAF/ncBAF chromatin remodeling complex subunit) to blood pressure. Without any human genetic association studies, functional data, or animal models in the record, the relationship cannot be classified as Established, Existing, or Hypothesized. The absence of supporting citations points most strongly to a Novel designation, with small residual probability reflecting the possibility that GWAS catalog entries exist but were not supplied here.

No human genetic study in this set reports OPN5 variants associated with BMI or obesity; the human-based papers concern opsin expression in skin, melanocytic tumor variants, and neuronal differentiation, none with adiposity phenotypes. The strongest relevant evidence is the mouse study showing Opn5-expressing hypothalamic preoptic neurons suppress brown adipose tissue thermogenesis, with Opn5-null mice showing overactive BAT and increased body temperature (PMID 32879486), plus a related POA thermoregulatory clock study (PMID 35957988) — these provide a plausible energy-balance mechanism but are animal data. A sheep GWAS lists OPN5 as a candidate for productivity/exterior traits (PMID 35087996), again non-human and only indirectly related to body composition. Therefore the evidence supports a biologically plausible but not variant-based human link, i.e., Hypothesized, with some residual chance that the co-mentions are considered incidental (Novel).

None of the provided articles report any human genetic variant in WASHC1 associated with blood pressure or hypertension; there are no GWAS, family, or cohort studies linking the gene to blood pressure, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The literature is dominated by cell-biological work on the WASH complex in endosomal recycling, actin nucleation, immune synapse formation, replication stress, and Drosophila oogenesis (PMIDs 28646090, 34423835, 35733063, 29549166, 34486665, 42233622), which are mechanistically unrelated to vascular tone. The only cardiometabolically relevant evidence is from mouse models showing hepatic and intestinal Washc1 ablation alters LDL/HDL cholesterol handling and intestinal cholesterol absorption (PMIDs 31167970, 38086439); these are animal studies and concern lipids, not blood pressure, giving at most a weak indirect cardiovascular rationale. The keratinocyte cancer exome study (PMID 37444464) mentions a WASHC1 variant but for an unrelated phenotype. Accordingly, most probability falls on Novel, with a modest allocation to Hypothesized based on the murine lipid/receptor-trafficking biology.

No articles were supplied, so there is no citable evidence in this set demonstrating that ANKDD1B variants cause or associate with type 2 diabetes, and no functional or animal-model data linking the gene to glucose homeostasis. Without at least one human genetic study reporting an association, the "Established" category is impossible (no PMIDs can be named showing variants in independent probands or families), and "Existing" cannot be documented here either. Some probability is retained for "Existing" because ANKDD1B lies in a chromosome 5 locus that has been reported in lipid and cardiometabolic GWAS, which could plausibly include diabetes-related traits, and for "Hypothesized" on similar grounds. Based solely on the provided (empty) literature, the most defensible classification is Novel.

None of the provided articles examine bipolar disorder; there are no association studies, CNV analyses, or sequencing reports linking MACROD2 variants to bipolar probands or families. The evidence base concerns other phenotypes: autism spectrum disorder (GWAS hit rs4141463, largely non-replicated), ADHD rare CNVs, epilepsy, obesity, congenital heart disease, thyroid orbitopathy, and brain structure. The closest psychiatric signals are rare CNVs in MACROD2 in major depressive disorder patients with suicide attempts (not genome-wide significant) and cross-disorder neurodevelopmental CNV findings, which at best support a general, non-specific neuropsychiatric role rather than a bipolar-specific one. Because MACROD2 is brain-expressed and influences temporal lobe volume and other psychiatric phenotypes, a biologically plausible (hypothesized) link can be argued, but direct human genetic evidence for bipolar disorder is absent, so Novel is the most likely classification.
